# Efficiently Representing Algorithms with Chain-of-Thought Transformers **Abstract** The increasing popularity of _reasoning_ models--language models that output a series of reasoning or thought tokens before producing an answer--is justified, in part, by theoretical results showing that chain-of-thought (CoT) transformers can simulate Turing machines, and thus perform arbitrary computation. However, the Turing machine, while suitable for complexity-theoretic analysis, is not convenient, intuitive, or efficient for discussing algorithms. Algorithms are typically designed and analyzed at a higher level of abstraction, captured by the _Word RAM_ model with random-access memory and unit-cost operations on O(log_n_)-bit words. As a result, Word RAM algorithms can be substantially more efficient than their Turing machine counterparts, raising the question: _Can CoT transformers efficiently simulate Word RAM algorithms?_ For instance, can they sort _n_ items in O(_n_log_n_) steps or run Dijkstra’s algorithm in O(_E+V_log_V_) steps? We answer affirmatively, up to polylogarithmic overhead. We first establish this for finite-precision transformers with poly-logarithmic width and rightmost unique hard attention, then strengthen the result to two more practical settings with finite width and log-precision: _continuous_ CoT, where reasoning takes the form of vectors rather than tokens, and a _hybrid_ architecture in which transformer layers sit atop a recurrent (linear RNN) layer. In all three cases, we find that CoT _can_ efficiently simulate any Word RAM algorithm with only a poly-logarithmic overhead in _n_. This overhead reduces to log-square when the Word RAM has a “flat” instruction set, and only logarithmic for multiplication-free flat instructions--in stark contrast to known CoT simulations of Turing machines, which require quadratic overhead over Word RAM. ### 1 Introduction It has been known for a while that chain of thought (CoT) makes transformers _Turing complete_--able to simulate any algorithm in principle (Pérez et al., 2021). This justifies the empirical practice of training reasoning models to solve complex tasks (e.g., Snell et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; OpenAI, 2026). However, the ability to simulate a Turing machine (TM) does not immediately translate to being able to implement interpretable algorithms efficiently: while TMs provide an established framework for analyzing computational complexity, they are not practical for designing real-world algorithms. For instance, sorting _n_ items takes only O(_n_log_n_) steps on a random-access machine (RAM)--an idealized computer whose memory cells can be read and written in unit time at arbitrary addresses, formalized in §2.1--because each comparison and swap touches an arbitrary array entry in a single step. A TM has no such random access: to reach the addressed cell it must move its head there, scanning a tape region of length up to O(_n+t_) per access. <tbc>O(_n_log_n_) RAM steps on a TM therefore costs up to O(_n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_) steps, and on a single-tape TM sorting provably requires \(\Omega(n^2/logn)\) steps (Hennie, 1965). This overhead is not a quirk of the analysis--it reflects a fundamental mismatch between TMs and algorithms that rely on random memory access or word-level arithmetic. This paper asks: can CoT transformers efficiently simulate algorithms as written in textbooks? We answer affirmatively.

The natural model for describing textbook algorithms efficiently and concisely is the **Word RAM**. A Word RAM program stores data in a random-access memory (RAM) partitioned into _words_ of \(w=\Theta(log(n+t))\) bits--wide enough to address any of the O(_n+t_) cells the program may touch during a _t_-step execution--and it executes a program one instruction at a time, where each instruction runs in O(1) steps. Its primitive operations--memory reads and writes, integer arithmetic, bitwise operations, and comparisons--correspond directly to the operations of modern programming languages and the algorithms textbooks describe. Thus, the standard complexity bounds practitioners know about correspond naturally to the algorithms expressed in the Word RAM model. For example, sorting takes O(_n_log_n_) Word RAM steps and Dijkstra’s algorithm takes O(_E+V_log_V_).

Existing CoT expressivity results establish computational universality by simulating Turing machines (Pérez et al., 2021; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024). These constructions, however, operate entirely at the TM-instruction level: each CoT token encodes one tape symbol, and each decoding step simulates one TM transition. Routing a Word RAM program of _t_ steps through this construction therefore costs O(_t_<sup>2</sup>) CoT tokens: a Word RAM on a TM already incurs an O(_t_<sup>2</sup>) blowup,<sup>1</sup> and the CoT spends one token per TM step. What is missing is a direct simulation at the Word RAM-instruction level--one that would let CoT transformers execute textbook algorithms at close to their textbook complexity.

We close this gap with direct Word RAM simulations for decoder-only CoT transformers in three settings. _(i)_ First, finite-precision transformers of polylogarithmic width using rightmost-unique hard attention--an interpretable and pedagogical construction emitting O(_w_<sup>2</sup>) tokens per Word RAM instruction, hence O(_tw_<sup>2</sup>)=O(_t_log<sup>2</sup>(_n+t_)) tokens overall, with the per-instruction overhead dropping to O(_w_) for multiplication-free instruction sets. This is essentially tight for discrete CoT: just as a Python program hard-coding a _p_-bit integer must write \(\Omega(p)\) characters, any CoT transcript representing a _w_-bit word must emit \(\Omega(w)\) tokens from a fixed alphabet, giving an \(\Omega(tw)=\Omega(tlog(n+t))\) lower bound. Our Word RAM simulation matches this bound up to one logarithmic factor in general and exactly when multiplication is excluded--already far below the \(\Omega(t^2)\) of TM-based CoT simulations. _(ii)_ Second, _fixed-width_ transformers with _continuous CoT_--which reasons with hidden vectors in place of discrete tokens. These models can invoke a TM oracle for each Word RAM instruction, generalizing the finite-precision setting. _(iii)_ Third, _hybrid_ models--transformers augmented with a linear RNN layer--which can implement the same simulation with _explicit_ CoT. For an instruction set whose individual operations run in time \(\kappa(w)\) on a TM, the latter two constructions take \(\mathcal{O}(t\kappa(w))\) CoT steps, generalizing the results to arbitrary instruction sets. This recovers the same poly-logarithmic overhead as the first setting: for the flat instruction sets we consider, \(\kappa(w)=\mathcal{O}(w)\) when multiplication, division, and modulo are excluded and O(_w_<sup>2</sup>) otherwise, so \(\mathcal{O}(t\kappa(w))\) is O(_t_log(_n+t_)) or O(_t_log<sup>2</sup>(_n+t_)) accordingly.

## 2 Preliminaries

### 2.1 The Word RAM Computational Model

There are several different variants of Word RAMs in the literature with different instruction set details, ranging from C-like Word RAMs (Hagerup, 1998; Thorup, 1996; Morin, 2013) to the weaker multiplication-free basic instruction set of Brodnik et al. (1997). While classical literature has often explored various _minimal_, assembly-like instruction sets under which the model is Turing-complete, our goal here is different: we would like to argue that transformers and hybrid models, when equipped with CoT, can directly simulate programs even when they are written in a much higher-level language, such as "textbook algorithms" or simple Python programs, with only a log or log-square overhead. Note that this is a stronger claim than simulating a minimal instruction set with instructions like `load`, `store`, `increment`, etc., with a log or log-square overhead. Keeping this overhead small is important; after all, every Word RAM program can be converted to a Turing machine if one disregards the overhead (which, in general, would be quadratic), and then simulated using standard transformers with CoT via known constructions (Pérez et al., 2021; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024).

**Syntax.** To this end, we define the following grammar for specifying Word RAM programs. Let _n_ be the input length, _k_ as the maximum number of variables (realized as registers) allowed in the Word RAM program, and `c1, ..., cm` as the fixed constants (independent of _n_) allowed in the program.

We call a Word RAM program **flat** if it uses only the flat grammar above. We further distinguish two flat instruction classes by which operators from Op appear: **full-arithmetic** flat programs may use any operator from Op, while **simple-arithmetic** flat programs restrict Op to \(\{+,-,\checkmark,\gg,\&,|,\oplus\}\), i.e., it excludes \(\times\), \(\div\), mod.

**Semantics.** A specific Word RAM machine is specified by a finite-length program of the form above, with the standard semantics when executed on a string \(x\in\Sigma^*\). In more detail, the machine has three memory arrays: a read-only one `inp` that contains the input **_x_**, `mem` is a standard read-write tape initialized to all zeros, and `out` is an output tape that can only be written to, where written values are stored \(\mathrm{mod}|\Sigma|\). The machine state also specifies the value of the program counter `pc` and finite registers `r1`_,...,_`rk`, which all start as 0. When an instruction is run, `pc` is incremented, unless it is otherwise assigned by the instruction (e.g., `pc`=`r2`+1). The program runs until `halt` is executed, at which point the contents of `out` is deemed the output. When considering language recognition, we say that a Word RAM accepts a string iff `out`\[0\]=1.

Without loss of generality, we can view the program counter `pc` and each register `ri` as stored in memory via \(\mathtt{pc}\unknown\mathtt{mem}[0]\) and \(\mathtt{ri}\unknown\mathtt{mem}[-i]\), with `mem` being 1-indexed for standard memory.

## 2.2 Transformers and Related Models

**Transformers.** We defer a definition of the standard transformers model to §A.1. The depth of our transformer will be _fixed_, i.e., O(1), w.r.t. sequence length _n_ and CoT runtime _t_=O(_n<sup>c</sup>_). Regarding precision and width of our transformers, we consider two possibilities motivated by a bifurcation in the transformer expressivity literature (Strobl et al., 2024; Svete et al., 2026):

1. Fixed precision and polylogarithmic, i.e., O(log_<sup>k</sup>n_) width. Because width grows with _n_ and _t_, this model is not fully uniform, meaning new parameters are introduced on longer inputs and CoTs. We use rightmost-unique hard attention transformers ( UHATS) (cf. Strobl et al., 2024).<tbc>

2. Logarithmic, i.e., O(log_n_), precision and fixed width. We further enforce in this model that the parameters are fully uniform. We use averaging hard attention (cf. Strobl et al., 2024).

**Linear RNNs and Hybrid Models.** Next, we define linear RNN layers. There are many existing linear RNN architectures with complex parameterizations that all meet the following general form for different choices of _A<sub>t</sub>_, _b<sub>t</sub>_, and _c<sub>t</sub>_ (Merrill et al., 2026): _S_<sub>_t_+1</sub>=_A<sub>t</sub>S<sub>t</sub>+b<sub>t</sub>_ and \(h_t=c_t^\top S_t\) We will assume for simplicity that _A<sub>t</sub>_, _b<sub>t</sub>_, and _c<sub>t</sub>_ are all parameterized as projections of the input vector to the RNN layer at step _t_. RNNs can be fit into a transformer architecture by using the head input to compute _A<sub>t</sub>,b<sub>t</sub>_, and _c<sub>t</sub>_ and then defining _h<sub>t</sub>_ as the head output. The sublayer output from a multihead RNN layer would then be passed through layer-norm in the standard way. A _hybrid model_ is an architecture that mixes attention heads with linear RNN heads.

**CoT.** Finally, we say that a transformer _T_ computes a function _f_ within CoT budget _t(n_) if, after feeding **_x_** through _T_ and allowing at most _t_(|_w_|) autoregressive steps sampled greedily (potentially terminating early), the generated tokens end with the suffix =_f(w_)$, where = is an output delimiter and $ is the end-of-string symbol. Continuous CoT is defined analogously except that final logits of the transformer are passed as a "soft token" to the next step rather than a token decoded from them.

## 2.3 Layernorm Hash Representation

In the log-precision model, we will represent values _v_ using their layer-norm hash \(\phi(v)\), which is a unit-norm vector in R<sup>4</sup> defined as follows (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024):

\(\phi(v)\equiv\phi(v,1):=\mathrm{layernorm}(v,1,-v,-1)=\frac{(v,1,-v,-1)}{\sqrt{2v^2+2}}.\) (1)

More generally, \(\phi(a,b)=\mathrm{layernorm}(a,b,-a,-b)\). This representation has several useful properties (similar to binary encodings) that we will leverage. The first property is useful for performing an equality check using inner product, as well as tie-breaking in order to simulate rightmost attention:

**Proposition 1** (Equality Check and Mismatch Gap: Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024)**.** _Let_ \(u,v\in\{0,1,\dots,T\}\)_. Then_ \(\langle\phi(u),\phi(v)\rangle=1\) _if and only if u=v. Further, when_ \(u\neq v\), \(\phi(u),\phi(v)\rangle\le 1-\delta_T\) _where_ \(\delta_T:=\frac{1}{4(T^2+1)^2}\).

See proof in §A.2 for completeness. \(\phi\) is scale invariant (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024): \(\phi(cu,cv)=\phi(u,v)=\phi(u/v,1)=\phi(u/v)\). We can also "swap" the dimensions of \(\phi\) to _invert_ a number: if \(\phi(v)=(s_1,s_2,-s_1,-s_2)\), then \(\phi(1/v)=(s_2,s_1,-s_2,-s_1)\). We introduce a new general _affine update_ (proof in §A.2), computable by a fixed-depth feedforward network as well as with an RNN:

**Proposition 2** (Affine Update)**.** _Fix constants_ \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\)_. Let_ \(\phi(v)=(s_1,s_2,-s_1,-s_2)\)_. Then_ \(\phi(av+b)=\mathrm{layernorm}(as_1+bs_2,s_2,-(as_1+bs_2),-s_2)\).

## 3 Simulating Word RAMs with Polylog-Width Transformers

We begin by showing how transformers with polylogarithmic width and fixed precision can simulate Word RAMs--a stepping stone towards more _uniform_ transformer models, which do not require new parameters as the input length grows. Thus, we use the construction in this section to cleanly outline the simulation; the main ideas will re-appear in the subsequent sections.

**The transformer model.** We use a log<sup>2</sup>-width finite-precision transformer model; see Remark 2 for a discussion of why log<sup>2</sup> width is needed. The constructions build on the log-width machinery formalized by existing work (Li et al., 2024; Svete et al., 2025; Svete and Sabharwal, 2026).<sup>2</sup> This allows us to reuse existing gadgets in our constructions.

**Representation of values.** In the polylogarithmic-width setting, word-sized integers are stored in the residual stream as binary vectors denoting their binary expansions: for a value \(v\in\{0,1\}^w\), the **representation** \(\mathrm{repr}(v)=^\mathrm{def}\mathrm{bits}(v)\in\{0,1\}^w\) is placed directly as a vector in the residual stream. This gives two primitives: _(i) equality checking_ via inner products (\(\mathrm{repr}(i)^\top\mathrm{repr}(j)=w\) iff _i=j_, and strictly less otherwise), and _(ii) bit extraction_ via \(\mathrm{repr}(v)^\top\mathbf{e}_t=b_t\) for the _t_th standard basis vector **_e_**_<sub>t</sub>_. These two primitives are the key gadgets exploited throughout this section; the subsequent sections will define different representations to maintain fixed width.

Thm. 1 formalizes Word RAM simulation by log<sup>2</sup>-width transformers; see §C for the full proof.

**Theorem 1** (Simulation of Word RAMs by log<sup>2</sup>-Width Transformers)**.** _Let M be a flat Word RAM program with word size w. Then there exists a rightmost UHAT T with finite precision,_ O(_w_) _heads each of width_ O(_w), and total model dimension_ O(_w_<sup>2</sup>)=O(log<sup>2</sup>(_n+t_))_, such that, for any_ \(t\ge n\)_, T can simulate t steps of M with_ \(t\cdot\mathcal{O}(w^2)\) _CoT steps. Further, if M does not use_ \(\times\), \(\div\)_, or_ mod_, T can simulate t steps of M with_ \(t\cdot\mathcal{O}(w)\) _CoT steps._

_Proof sketch._ Following the Word RAM definition (§2.1), the Word RAM state--program counter, registers, and memory--is folded into a single random-access memory `mem`. The construction logs every memory write to the CoT transcript as a _memory block_ of the form `mem` # bits(_a_) # bits(_v_) (Fig. 1). The central operation is the _memory read_ (Lem. 12): given a query address bits(_a_) in the residual stream, recover the value of the rightmost `mem` block whose address field encodes _a_ (i.e., the most recent write to `mem`\[_a_\]). This uses two attention steps: the first selects the rightmost matching address position; the second retrieves the value field at the known offset.

Each CoT step runs four constant-depth layer blocks (cf. Fig. 4 and §C): _(i)_ **Load pc:** an indexed read with the constant query 0 recovers bits(`mem`\[0\]) in two attention layers (Prop. 3); _(ii)_ **Load Instruction and Operands:** the active line of the program is identified from bits(`mem`\[0\]) by an MLP that issues parallel reads of every compile-time address listed in the instruction’s operand descriptor (registers), and a second round of reads resolves any runtime addresses (`mem`\[_a_\] or `inp`\[_a_\]) whose index _a_ is now in the residual stream (Prop. 4); _(iii)_ **Execute:** a single MLP computes the _w_-bit<tbc>

For simple instructions, Blocks _(i)-(iii)_ produce identical outputs at every token within the same step, so only \(\delta\) advances in Block _(iv)_, emitting one token at a time over O(_w_) total positions. Deserialization uses _w_ dedicated attention heads (one per bit), each of width _w_, giving the O(_w_<sup>2</sup>)=O(log<sup>2</sup>(_n+t_)) model dimension. In contrast to simple instructions, multiplication, division, and modulo _cannot_ be computed in a single transformer step and are compiled into O(_w_) flat micro-steps that share state through program-private memory cells. Each micro-step costs O(_w_) tokens, for O(_w_<sup>2</sup>) total; every micro-step uses the same four-block pipeline (Prop. 7).

**Corollary 1.** _Let M and T be as in Thm. 1. We have the following:_

(_i)_ _T can simulate t steps of M with_ full-arithmetic _flat instructions using_ O(_t_log<sup>2</sup>_t_) _steps._<tbc>

_(ii)_ _T can simulate t steps of M with_ simple-arithmetic _flat instructions using_ O(_t_log_t_) _steps._

_Remark_ 1 (Bit extraction as a dot product). Reading from and writing into the CoT transcript both require _bit extraction_: computing BIT(_v,t_), the _t_th bit of _v_. In the log<sup>2</sup>-width setting this is trivial: since \(\text{bits}(v)\in\{0,1\}^w\) is stored as a coordinate vector in the residual stream, extracting _b<sub>t</sub>_ reduces to the dot product \(\text{bits}(v)^\top\mathbf{e}_t=b_t\) with the _t_th standard basis vector **_e_**_<sub>t</sub>_. In the fixed-width constructions later, bits(_v_) is no longer directly available as a coordinate vector, so bit extraction becomes substantially more involved and is one of the primary sources of complexity in those proofs.

These results provide a general framework for how CoT can simulate Word RAM programs. However, the log<sup>2</sup>-width construction is _non-uniform_: the model grows with _n_, so new parameters--untrained on shorter inputs--must be invoked as the inputs grow longer. The construction also requires _rightmost_ UHAT; we show in Remark 3 that weaker attention models cannot implement the indexed- read step. The fixed-width constructions in the following sections avoid the non-uniformity and reliance on rightmost UHATs at the cost of more complex reading and writing mechanisms.

## 4 Towards a Uniform Fixed-Width Construction: Bottlenecks and Plan

In §3, storing bits(_v_) in the residual stream gives three things for free: _(i)_ equality checking via inner products, _(ii)_ bit extraction via \(\text{bits}(v)^\top\mathbf{e}_t=b_t\), and _(iii)_ a clean serialization/deserialization mechanism. Moving to fixed width forces us to abandon the bits representation, and each of these primitives must be rebuilt from scratch. We describe the resulting challenges below.

**Bottleneck: Reading and writing values.** The deepest challenge in moving to fixed width is that we must adopt a different representation of numbers in the residual stream. For fixed-width constructions, any such representation repr of values must satisfy two properties simultaneously:

(a) _Equality gap:_ \(\text{repr}(i)^\top\text{repr}(j)=1\) if _i=j_, and \(\text{repr}(i)^\top\text{repr}(j)<1-\epsilon\) otherwise.<tbc>

(b) _Read/write:_ We can serialize repr(_v_) to a binary CoT encoding and recover repr(_v_) from it.

The first property is needed for the indexed-read attention mechanism; the second is needed both _(a)_ to pass pointers computed at a higher layer back to lower layers in future steps, and _(b)_ to hand binary-encoded operands to the TM oracle for complex arithmetic. Past work has established the **layer-norm hash** \(\phi(i)\) as a fixed-width representation satisfying the equality-gap property (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024), but reading and writing via \(\phi\) presents a challenge.

Writing is hard because it requires computing BIT(_v,j_) from \(\phi(v)\)--mapping a hash representation back to individual bits.<sup>3</sup> One approach is to compute \(\phi(v\mathrm{mod}2)\) and \(\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\) iteratively. When \(v\le t\), Merrill and Sabharwal (2025) give a construction for computing \(\phi(v\mathrm{mod}2)\) and \(\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\) from \(\phi(v)\); for larger values this is open (note that Prop. 2 allows easily computing \(\phi(v/2)\), but not \(\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\)). To resolve the write challenge, we adopt a normal form for Word RAMs that enforces \(v\le t\) at every step, developed in §4.1, allowing us to compute the least significant bit of _v_ as well as \(\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\). The remaining bits of _v_ can be obtained by iterating the process, which requires repeatedly _conditioning_ on \(\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\), \(\phi(\lfloor v/4\rfloor)\), etc. We show this can be achieved via either of two minimal<tbc>

architectural extensions: continuous CoT (§5, Lem. 5) or hybrid transformer-RNN models (§6, Lem. 8).<sup>4</sup>

Reading is hard for a complementary reason: while \(\phi(v)\) can be reconstructed from a binary CoT encoding via iterative bit-shifting within the \(\phi\) representation, this is not known to be achievable by a plain transformer. We show that this too becomes feasible with either of two minimal architectural extensions: continuous CoT (§5, Lem. 7) and hybrid transformer-RNN models (§6, Lem. 9).<sup>4</sup>

### 4.1 Writing Solution: Equivalent RAMs with Bounded Word Values

We define a _c_**-dimensional** Word RAM as a Word RAM where the tape is replaced by a _c_-dimensional array of _c_-dimensional tuples. The following lemma shows that such Word RAMs are as powerful as standard Word RAMs, up to a constant factor in runtime (see §B for a proof):

**Lemma 1.** _Let M be a 1-dimensional Word RAM with word size w=c_log(_n+t_) _for some_ \(c\in\mathbb{N}\)_. Then there exists a c-dimensional restricted Word RAM_ \(M'\) _with word size_ \(w'=\mathrm{log}(n+t)\) _and the same instruction set as M that simulates t steps of M using_ O(_t_) _steps._

This shows that we can reduce any _M_ using word size _w=c_log(_n+t_) to \(M'\) using word size _w_=log(_n+t_). Now, define a Word RAM as **restricted** if, for any step _i_, any value _v_ represented in any register satisfies \(v\le i\). Any Word RAM _M_ can be converted to be restricted by making it do nothing for the first _v_ steps, and then simulating the _i_-th step of _M_ at step _v+i_:

**Lemma 2.** _Let M be any c-dimensional Word RAM where all values are at most v(n_) _on inputs of size n. Then there exists_ \(M'\) _that simulates t steps of M using v(n_)+_t steps such that, at each step i, all values in_ \(M'\) _are at most i._

We can first invoke Lem. 1 and then apply Lem. 2 with _v(n_)=_n+t_ to obtain the following:

**Theorem 2** (Restricted Word RAM Equivalence)**.** _A standard Word RAM running in time t(n_) _on inputs of size n can be simulated by a restricted c-dimensional Word RAM in time_ O(_n+t(n_)).

This will be useful because simulating restricted Word RAMs with transformer-like models will be easier than simulating unrestricted ones. Specifically, the property \(v\le i\) will be useful for writing numbers in binary as it allows us to divide numbers using attention via the following special case of the "division lemma" of Merrill and Sabharwal (2024) where the divisor is 2 (see §B for a proof):

**Lemma 3** (Simplified Division Lemma)**.** _There exists a transformer block that, for any_ \(\phi(v)\) _present in the residual stream at position t for_ \(v\le t\)_, adds_ \(\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\) _and_ \(\phi(v\mathrm{mod}2)\) _to the residual stream._

This will be useful for writing numbers \(\phi(v)\) onto the CoT in binary because it allows computing the least significant bit via \(\phi(v\mathrm{mod}2)\), or \(\phi(v\mathrm{mod}2^i)\), which can be useful for recovering other bits.

## 5 Simulating Word RAMs with Continuous CoT

The bounded-value normal form from §4.1 ensures a crucial _bit-extraction_ precondition: during execution, every word _v_ at RAM step _s_ satisfies \(v\le s\). Since each simulated step produces at least one transcript symbol, this implies \(v\le\tau\) whenever the simulator begins emitting a bit-string segment at transcript position \(\tau\). Thus, whenever we need to stream a word as bits we may apply the simplified division primitive (Lem. 3) to compute \(\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\) and \(\phi(v\mathrm{mod}2)\) (the first bit) from \(\phi(v)\), and then repeat the process for the next bit by _conditioning_ the computation on \(\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\), and so on.

The remaining obstacle is _persistence_: after streaming _w_ discrete bits, later computation must still have access to a constant-dimensional _word code_ that supports exact-match attention (for RAM addressing) and can be carried forward across time.

We show that _continuous CoT_ can be used to achieve both conditioning and persistence.

**Continuous CoT and soft tokens.** In the continuous-CoT model, each decoding step emits both (i) a discrete token from a fixed alphabet and (ii) a constant-dimensional _soft token_ \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d_s}\). The next decoding step receives the entire prefix, including the past soft tokens, so _p<sub>i</sub>_ can be attended to by future layers. In particular, a constant-depth transformer block can copy designated coordinates of<tbc>

<sup>4</sup>This iterative computation can also be performed by a logarithmic-depth transformer; we do not explore this here.

the most recent soft token forward (e.g. via a fixed-offset retrieval head), so the soft token acts as a small persistent register bank threaded through the transcript.

**Theorem 3** (Simulating Word RAMs with CCoT)**.** _Let M be a d-dimensional-array Word RAM with word size w_=log(_n+t_)+O(1) _and per-instruction bit-serial cost bound_ \(\kappa(w)\).<sup>5</sup> _Then there exists a log-precision, finite-width_ continuous CoT _transformer T such that, for any_ \(t\ge n\)_, t steps of M can be simulated by T using_ \(\mathcal{O}(t\kappa(w))\) _decoding steps._

_Proof overview._ We prove Thm. 3 by induction on the simulated RAM step _s_. The simulator maintains an _append-only_ transcript whose soft token stores the pair \((\phi(a),\phi(v))\) for the written address/value \(\mathtt{mem}[a]\leftarrow v\) (absorbing `pc` and registers into `mem`; see §2.1). Checkpoint and store- summary positions are marked by constant discrete tags so attention can restrict to the relevant subset. If no store-summary exists for an address _a_, the value at `mem`\[_a_\] is interpreted as 0. A useful property of continuous CoT is that we can always make the latest checkpoint available "from layer 0" at future positions: a constant-depth carry block can attend to the rightmost checkpoint tag and copy its soft-token coordinates into designated coordinates of the current residual stream.

**One simulated RAM step.** Assume the invariant holds at the end of RAM step _s_. To simulate step _s_+1, we perform the following conceptual phases (some happen within a single decoding step, others take many decoding steps), illustrated in Fig. 2:

(1) _Load `pc`._ Attend to the rightmost checkpoint and copy \(\phi(\mathrm{PC}^{(s)})\) (and the register codes) into the current residual stream. Use PC<sup>(_s_)</sup> to select which instruction subroutine/oracle to run.<tbc>

(2) _Load operand values._ For each register/constant operand, read \(\phi(\cdot)\) directly from the copied checkpoint state. For each memory operand `mem`\[_a_\], form \(\phi(a)\) and dereference the most recent matching store-summary to recover the operand in coded form \(\phi(v)\) (Lemma 4).<tbc>

(3) _Serialize inputs (write a binary tape)._ For each coded input word needed by the instruction oracle, emit its _w_ bits onto the discrete transcript using Lemma 5. This creates a delimited _work-tape suffix_ for the instruction oracle.<tbc>

(4) _Instruction execution (TM oracle)._ Activate the instruction-specific TM-oracle subroutine, which operates only on the work-tape suffix and runs for \(\mathcal{O}(\kappa(w))\) decoding steps, emitting the output words as bit streams (Lemma 6).<tbc>

(5) _Deserialize outputs._ Convert each output bit stream into its coded form \(\phi(\cdot)\) for future addressing and equality tests, using Lemma 7.<tbc>

(6) _Store updates (re-establish the invariant)._ Emit a new checkpoint token whose soft token stores the updated state \(\phi(\mathrm{PC}^{(s+1)}),\phi(r_1^{(s+1)}),\dots,\phi(r_\rho^{(s+1)})\). By construction, this new checkpoint (and store-summary, if present) is the rightmost such entry, so it will be used at the next step.

Correctness follows from induction on _s_: step (5) appends the new rightmost checkpoint encoding the updated registers/PC, and appends the new rightmost store-summary for any updated address. ## 7 Conclusion

We show that poly-logarithmic-width transformers can simulate a Word RAM; while it is unclear whether fixed-width transformers can also do so, we show that two minimal extensions to fixed-width transformers (continuous CoT transformers and hybrid models) both can. Our results show that CoT--at least for certain architectures--allows simulating algorithms with their general textbook runtimes up to a polylogarithmic factor, removing the quadratic overhead that would be incurred by going through previously established Turing completeness results (Pérez et al., 2021; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024). Since certain realistic extensions (continuous CoT or RNN layers) to transformers are crucial for the fixed-width constructions, it is an interesting open question to what degree these extensions are necessary for efficient Word RAM simulation. It would also be interesting to study to what degree these extensions benefit algorithmic reasoning in transformer models in practice.

<tbc>Then<tbc>

**Lemma 1.** _Let M be a 1-dimensional Word RAM with word size w=c_log(_n+t_) _for some_ \(c\in\mathbb{N}\)_. _Proof._ We will show how to simulate _M_ with \(M'\). The following invariant will be helpful: _M_ has size \(w=cw'\), so any value _x_ can represented with _c_ values \(x'_1,\dots,x'_c\), each of word size \(w'\).

For any instruction in _M_ that retrieves the value at _x_ and stores it into _y_, we will instead have _c_ instructions that retrieve the value at each \(x'_i\) and store it into \(y'_i\) for \(1\le i\le c\). Similarly, whenever we write the value at _y_ into _x_, we will have _c_ instructions that write value \(y'_i\) into \(x'_i\). Thus, each read or write instruction in _M_ can be simulated by _c_ instructions in \(M'\).

It remains to be shown that arithmetic instructions in _M_ can also be simulated in \(M'\):

• _Adding x_ and _y_ in _M_ can be implemented in \(M'\) by starting with \(\kappa_1=0\) and adding blocks \(x'_i+y'_i+\kappa_i\) iteratively for _i_=1,2_,...,c_, with \(\kappa_{i+1}=\unknown[x'+y'\ge 2^w]\) being the carry bit for the subsequent step. This takes at most 2_c_ steps.<tbc>

• _Subtracting_ mirrors addition, with the _borrow_ bit \(\beta_{i+1}=\unknown[x'+\beta_i<y']\). (If the final borrow bit \(\beta_{c+1}=1\), the result is negative.)<tbc>

• _Multiplying x_ and _y_ in _M_ can be implemented in \(M'\) via long multiplication in base \(m=2^{w^\prime}\). Write \(x=\sum_{i=1}^cx'_i\cdot m^{i-1}\) and \(y=\sum_{j=1}^cy'_j\cdot m^{j-1}\). For each _j_=1_,...,c_, we compute the partial product \(a_j=x\cdot y'_j\cdot m^{j-1}\) and keep a running sum \(S\leftarrow S+a_j\). The partial product \(x\cdot y'_j\) is itself computed block-by-block: for each _i_=1_,...,c_, multiply \(x'_i\cdot y'_j\) (a product of two \(w'\)-bit numbers, fitting in \(2w'\) bits) and add it into block _i_ of the partial product together with any carry from block _i_-1. Since each \(x'_i,y'_j<2^{w^\prime}\), the product \(x'_i\cdot y'_j<2^{2w^\prime}\), so the carry into block _i_+1 is at most \(2^{w^\prime}-1\), which fits in \(w'\) bits. Computing one partial product \(x\cdot y'_j\) thus takes _O(c_) steps; summing it into _S_ (via the addition procedure above) takes another _O(c_) steps. Over all _c_ values of _j_, the total cost is _O(c_<sup>2</sup>) steps.<tbc>

• _Dividing x_ by _y_ in _M_ can be implemented in \(M'\) via long division in base \(m=2^{w^\prime}\), analogously to multiplication (Knuth, 1997, §4.3.1, Alg. D). The quotient \(\lfloor x/y\rfloor\) has _c_ base-_m_ digits \(q'_1,\dots,q'_c\); we recover them one by one from most to least significant. At each step, the top two blocks of the running remainder and the top block of _y_ together determine the next quotient digit exactly via a single \(w'\)-bit division (available as a primitive in \(M'\)). Each of the _c_ digits thus costs O(_c_) steps (one scalar division plus a multiply-and-subtract to update the remainder), giving O(_c_<sup>2</sup>) total.<tbc>

In their construction, each position _i_ computes \(\phi(i/m)\) and performs an equality test with \(\phi(j)\) computed at all prior positions _j\<i_ to determine if _i/m_ is an integer, i.e., _i_ is a multiple of _m_. Then position _t_ attends back to find the closest multiple of _m_ via rightmost hard attention to compute the mod and div values.

In our special use case, we can simplify this process as follows: each position _j\<t_ computes a key \(k_j=\phi(2j)\) and value \(\phi(j)\). Position _t_ uses query \(q_t=\phi(v-1)\), which can be computed via Prop. 2. It can be verified that the closest matching key is \(k_{\lceil(v-1)/2\rceil}\),<sup>7</sup> and the corresponding value is \(\phi(\lceil(v-1)/2\rceil)\). Observe that for all integer values _v_, \(\lceil(v-1)/2\rceil=\lfloor v/2\rfloor\). Thus the retrieved value is \(\phi(\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\), which we add to the residual stream. To obtain \(\phi(vmod2)\), we compute \(\phi(2\lfloor v/2\rfloor)\) via Prop. 2 and perform an equality test with \(\phi(v)\). If these are equal, \(\phi(vmod2)\) is 0, otherwise it is 1; we add this to the residual stream as well.

## C Proofs of Polylog-Width Transformer Results

### Serialization format.

Before stating the propositions, we fix the transcript format used throughout all four components.

<sup>7</sup>Suppose _v_ is odd, i.e., _v_=2_j_<sup>∗</sup>+1 for some integer _j_<sup>∗</sup>. Then (_v_-1)/2=_j_<sup>∗</sup> and we have an exact key-query match between _q<sub>t</sub>_ and _k_<sub>_j_<sup>∗</sup></sub>. When _v_ is even, say _v_=2_j_<sup>∗</sup>, then (_v_-1)/2=_j_<sup>∗</sup>-1/2. The two contenders for the closest match with \(q_t=\phi(2j^*-1)\) in this case are \(k_{j^*-1}=\phi(2j^*-2)\) and \(k_{j^*}=\phi(2j^*)\). Since these are unit norm vectors, the key-query inner product is the same as cosine distance, which is larger between \(\phi(2j^*-1)\) and \(\phi(2j^*)\) than between \(\phi(2j^*-1)\) and \(\phi(2j^*-2)\).

**Alphabet.** The output alphabet is \(\Sigma\sqcup\{0,1,\#,\&,\mathtt{mem}\}\), where & is the _end-of-step_ marker, `mem` is the _memory-write_ marker, and `0,1` are _bit tokens_. The simulator uses no other key tokens: the program counter, registers, and any instruction-private intermediate state all live in `mem` at fixed addresses (cf. §2.1), so every committed write has the same shape.

**Memory blocks.** Every write to the simulated memory appends one _memory block_ to the transcript:

\(\mathtt{mem}\underbrace{\# a_1\cdots a_w}_\mathtt{addressfield}\underbrace{\# v_1\cdots v_w}_\mathtt{valuefield},\)

occupying 2_w_+3 consecutive positions and recording \(\mathtt{mem}[a]\leftarrow v\). Lem. 12 matches an address bits(_a_) available in the residual stream against the address field of the rightmost `mem` block, then uses the known offset _w_+1 to retrieve the value field.

**Steps.** A Word RAM step is the run of (constant-many) memory blocks committed by one simulated instruction, terminated by an & token; & is therefore both an end-of-step marker and the anchor at which Blocks 1-3 produce the snapshot for the next step (see Block 4).

**Residual stream convention.** Throughout the proofs, the phrase "bits(_v_) is available in the residual stream at position _i_" means that the _w_-dimensional vector \(\text{bits}(v)=(b_1,\dots,b_w)\in\{0,1\}^w\) occupies a dedicated _w_-dimensional subspace of the \(\Theta(log^2n)\)-dimensional residual stream at that position. Each transformer layer reads from and writes to named subspaces; different subspaces hold different operands, intermediate addresses, and result slots so that they do not interfere. This can be done without loss of generality (Yang et al., 2026, §4.2).

**State recovery.** The contents of `mem`\[_a_\] at any point in the transcript is the value of the rightmost memory block whose address field encodes _a_. Lem. 12 performs this lookup in constant depth, writing the retrieved bits(_v_) into a designated residual-stream subspace.<sup>8</sup>

**Default values for unwritten cells.** At the start of simulation no memory block has been emitted, so a rightmost-match read for any address returns **0**. The Word RAM program supplies a static initialization vector that fixes the initial value at every address used by the program (zero by default; specific constants for `mem`\[0\]=PC<sub>start</sub> and any program-private scratch cells), and this initialization is baked into the transformer weights. When a read for address _a_ has no matching block in the transcript (detected by a single attention head testing whether the rightmost match exists), an MLP overrides the default **0** output of Lem. 12 with the program-specified initialization constant for that address. Because the initialization map is fixed at compile time and depends only on the program, this override is a constant-depth, finite-precision operation.

We now outline the proof of Thm. 1, which is the main result of this section; the propositions that follow will fill in the details of each component.

**Theorem 1** (Simulation of Word RAMs by log<sup>2</sup>-Width Transformers)**.** _Let M be a flat Word RAM program with word size w. Then there exists a rightmost UHAT T with finite precision,_ O(_w_) _heads each of width_ O(_w), and total model dimension_ O(_w_<sup>2</sup>)=O(log<sup>2</sup>(_n+t_))_, such that, for any_ \(t\ge n\)_, T can simulate t steps of M with_ \(t\cdot\mathcal{O}(w^2)\) _CoT steps. Further, if M does not use_ \(\times\), \(\div\)_, or_ mod_, T can simulate t steps of M with_ \(t\cdot\mathcal{O}(w)\) _CoT steps._

_Proof._ **Memory-only state.** Following the Word RAM definition (§2.1), the entire machine state-- program counter, registers, and the memory--is stored as a single random-access memory `mem` indexed by integer addresses. The transformer simulates the Word RAM by maintaining, in the CoT transcript, a log of memory writes from which the current contents of any address can be recovered. Concretely, every write to an address _a_ is appended to the transcript as a _memory block_

\(\mathtt{mem}\#\text{bits}(a)\#\text{bits}(v),\)

where \(\text{bits}(\cdot)\) is the binary encoding into {0,1}_<sup>w</sup>_. The contents of `mem`\[_a_\] at any point in the transcript is the value _v_ of the rightmost memory block whose address field encodes _a_, or the program-supplied initialization constant if no such block exists; Lem. 12 shows that a rightmost UHAT can perform this lookup in constant depth. Read-only input is handled identically: `inp`\[_i_\] is recovered by direct positional attention to input position _i_. The transcript is partitioned by & markers into _steps_, each step being the run of memory blocks committed by one simulated Word RAM instruction; see Fig. 4.

<sup>8</sup>This is analogous to the commonly studied _induction heads_ (Olsson et al., 2022): a head first matches the address pattern, then retrieves the value at the position immediately following it.

**What one CoT step does.** The construction decomposes each CoT step into four consecutive _layer blocks_, each handled by a constant-depth subnetwork.

**Block 1: Load pc (Prop. 3).** A single indexed read (Lem. 12) with query address 0 retrieves bits(mem[0]) from the transcript, recovering the current pc value into a dedicated residual-stream subspace. The indexed read uses two attention layers (address matching against the rightmost mem block with _a_=0, then value retrieval).

**Block 2: Load Instruction and Operands (Prop. 4).** Each instruction _I<sub>p</sub>_ in the program declares a fixed _operand descriptor_--a static list of memory addresses it reads--which the program supplies and is hard-coded into the transformer weights. The list contains two kinds of addresses: _compile-time_ addresses (the registers -_i_ and any program-private scratch cells used by _I<sub>p</sub>_) and _runtime_ addresses (memory or input cells whose index mem[_a_] or `inp[a_] is itself the value of another address that must be read first).

_Sub-step 2b (runtime reads)._ For each runtime address listed in _I<sub>p</sub>_’s descriptor (the value bits(_a_) for a mem\[_a_\] or `inp`\[_a_\] access), bits(_a_) is now available in the residual stream from Sub-step 2a. A second indexed read uses bits(_a_) as the query: Lem. 12 for mem\[_a_\], or a direct positional attention to input position _a_ for `inp`\[_a_\]. After Block 2 every operand of _I<sub>p</sub>_ resides in its designated residual-stream slot.

**Block 3: Execute Instruction (Prop. 5).** With all operands in the residual stream, a single constant- depth MLP computes the _w_-bit destination value bits(_v_) and the next `pc` value \(\text{bits}(\text{\texttt{pc}}')\), placing both into dedicated result slots. For instructions whose result is a _w_-bit function of _w_-bit operands (bitwise, +, -, \(\checkmark\), \(\gg\), comparisons, conditional moves, branch-target arithmetic), Block 3 implements the operation as an AC<sup>0</sup> circuit and uses no attention. For \(\times\), \(\div\), mod, Block 3 executes _one inner iteration_ of the corresponding long-multiplication or long-division algorithm; the per-iteration intermediates (partial product, remainder, quotient, phase counter) live in program-private memory cells, so they are read and written like any other word and the simulator-level treatment is unchanged (Prop. 7).

**Block 4: Store Results (Prop. 6).** Block 4 appends, to the transcript, the memory blocks committed by the active instruction: a `mem` # bits(_a<sub>d</sub>_) # bits(_v_) block for each address _a<sub>d</sub>_ that _I<sub>p</sub>_ writes (typically the destination plus the updated `pc`), followed by a closing &. The transformer’s weights are shared across positions, so Blocks 1-3 _run_ at every position; their reads are reliable, however, only at & positions, where the rightmost-match reads see exclusively committed memory blocks from _prior_ steps. At any non-& position within the current step’s serialization, a rightmost-match read for the destination address _a<sub>d</sub>_ would retrieve the freshly (and partially) written value of the current step rather than its operand-time value. Block 4 sidesteps this by ignoring the local outputs of Blocks 1-3 at non-& positions and instead attending to the most recent &, copying the snapshot (the addresses to be written and the corresponding result bits) that Blocks 1-3 produced at that &. B.1). When the offset hits a block boundary, the next memory block’s `mem` and # tokens are emitted; when all blocks have been written, the closing & is emitted, at which point Blocks 1-3 will again run on a clean prefix and produce the snapshot for the next step.

**Token count.** Each Word RAM step writes a constant number _K_ of memory blocks (depending only on the program, not the input), so

\(Cw+D=2Kw+3K+1\)

tokens are emitted per step (each block is `mem`, two #s, and 2_w_ bit tokens; one closing &). For instructions whose semantics is a single AC<sup>0</sup> operation (simple-arithmetic class) this is O(_w_) per step. For \(\times\)/\(\div\)/mod, the operation is unfolded into _w_ inner iterations, each of which is itself a flat memory-read/write step taking O(_w_) tokens (Prop. 7); the total is therefore O(_w_<sup>2</sup>). Summing over _t_ Word RAM steps gives \(t\cdot\mathcal{O}(w^2)\) CoT tokens, and \(t\cdot\mathcal{O}(w)\) when no \(\times\)/\(\div\)/mod instruction is used.

**Residual stream as a serialized snapshot.** It is instructive to view the residual stream at any CoT position as a structured record with one _w_-dimensional slot per memory block to be emitted by the current step: an address slot and a value slot for each of the _K_ writes. Each CoT token fills one bit of one slot, advancing \(\delta\) through the slots until & marks completion. The CoT transcript is therefore a sequence of `mem`-anchored memory blocks, and the simulator’s job at each step reduces to (i) reading a constant number of `mem` blocks, (ii) computing the new contents, and (iii) appending a constant number of new `mem` blocks. Fig. 4 (right) illustrates this view alongside the transcript structure.

**Proposition 3** (Load `pc`)**.** _Let T be a rightmost UHAT with_ log<sup>2</sup> _width and finite precision, and suppose the serialization format above is in use. At every CoT position t, T can recover_ bits(_mem_\[0\]) _from the transcript and place it in a dedicated residual-stream subspace using two attention layers._

_Proof._ The query address is the constant 0, hard-coded into the transformer weights and available in the residual stream as bits(0). A single application of Lem. 12 with this query retrieves bits(mem\[0\]): the first attention layer matches the rightmost `mem` block whose address field encodes 0 and extracts the position of the matching block; the second attention layer attends to the value field of that block and assembles its bits, via Lem. 11, into the dedicated bits(`pc`) subspace. If no such block exists, the override of the previous paragraph produces the program-supplied initial `pc` value bits(PC<sub>start</sub>).

**Proposition 4** (Load instruction and operands)**.** _Let T be a rightmost UHAT with_ log<sup>2</sup> _width and finite precision, and suppose_ bits(_mem_\[0\]) _is in the residual stream (from Block 1). Then T can identify the active instruction and load all its operands into designated residual-stream slots in four attention layers._

_Proof._ **Operand descriptor.** Every flat Word RAM instruction _I<sub>p</sub>_ is equipped with a static _operand descriptor_: a list of memory addresses to read. The descriptor partitions the addresses into

• _compile-time addresses_ \(A_p^\text{ct}\subseteq[2^w-1]\): integer constants known at program-compile time (the registers -_i_, the `pc` address 0, and any program-private scratch addresses used by _I<sub>p</sub>_);<tbc>

• _runtime addresses_ \(A_p^\text{rt}\): addresses of the form `mem`\[_a_\] or `inp`\[_a_\] where _a_ itself is the value at some compile-time address.

The descriptor is a _compile-time constant_: it depends only on the instruction type, not on the runtime values, so it is hard-coded into the weights of _T_.

**Sub-step 2a: Instruction identification and compile-time reads.** With bits(mem\[0\]) in the residual stream, a constant-depth MLP computes the match bit

\(\delta_p=^\text{def}\unknown[bits(mem[0])=bits(p)]\in\{0,1\}\)

for every program address \(p\in\{0,\dots,P-1\}\) simultaneously (each bits(_p_) is a hard-coded weight constant). The weights of _T_ contain _P_ attention-head groups H<sub>0</sub>_,...,_H<sub>_P_-1</sub>, one per program line. All _P_ groups run in parallel: each group H_<sub>p</sub>_ issues, for every compile-time address \(a\in A_p^\text{ct}\), one indexed read via Lem. 12 with the constant query bits(_a_), writing the retrieved bits(mem\[_a_\]) into a dedicated disjoint subspace of the residual stream. Each indexed read uses two attention layers (address matching, then value retrieval), and all _P_ groups run as parallel heads within those same two layers. A subsequent MLP gated by \(\delta_p\) copies the active group’s operands from their dedicated subspace into the shared operand slots, leaving the other subspaces unused. After Sub-step 2a, every compile-time operand of _I<sub>p</sub>_ occupies its designated slot.

**Sub-step 2b: Runtime reads.** For each runtime address in \(A_p^\text{rt}\), the address value bits(_a_) resolved in Sub-step 2a is now in the residual stream and serves as the query for a second indexed read: Lem. 12 for `mem`\[_a_\], or a direct positional attention to input position _a_ for `inp`\[_a_\]. By the _flat_ Word RAM constraint, no runtime address is itself memory-indirect, so two more attention layers suffice. After Sub-step 2b, all operands required by _I<sub>p</sub>_ reside in their designated residual-stream slots and are ready for Block 3.

The total depth of Block 2 is four attention layers plus a constant number of MLP layers.

**Proposition 5** (Execute instruction)**.** _Suppose all operands of instruction I<sub>p</sub> reside in their designated residual-stream slots (from Block 2). Then T can compute, in constant depth using a single MLP with no attention, the w-bit value_ bits(_v<sub>d</sub>_) _to be written to each address a<sub>d</sub> that I<sub>p</sub> updates, including the next `pc` value_ \(bits(\text{\textit{\textbf{pc}}}')\).

_Proof._ With all operands \(bits(a),bits(b)\in\{0,1\}^w\) in the residual stream, the active gated MLP subnetwork N_<sub>p</sub>_ computes the destination value(s) bits(_v<sub>d</sub>_) directly:

• _Bitwise operators_ (&, \(|,\oplus,\checkmark,\gg\)): each _v<sub>t</sub>_ is an _O_(1)-depth Boolean function of _a<sub>t</sub>_, _b<sub>t</sub>_ (and a hard-coded shift amount), computed in one MLP layer.<tbc>

• _Addition and subtraction_: implementable by a constant-depth AC<sup>0</sup> circuit (Straubing, 1994, §VIII.1), and thus by an MLP.<tbc>

• _Comparison_ (\(<,\le,=,\neq,\ge,>\)): reduced to subtraction and sign extraction.<tbc>

• _Boolean and conditional_ operations: computed in _O_(1) depth from the Boolean bits in the residual stream.<tbc>

• _Move and branch targets_: the result is a hard-coded constant or a copy of an operand value already in the residual stream.<tbc>

• _Inner iteration of_ \(\times\)/\(\div\)/mod: the MLP executes one iteration of the long-multiplication or long- division algorithm using the per-iteration intermediates (partial product, remainder, quotient, phase counter) read in Block 2 from program-private memory addresses, and produces their updated values as additional destination words (Prop. 7).

Block 3 always computes, in addition, the next `pc` value \(\mathrm{bits}(\mathrm{pc}')=\mathrm{bits}(\mathrm{mem}[0])+\mathrm{bits}(1)\) (or a hard-coded branch target if _I<sub>p</sub>_ is a branch); this value is written to address 0 by Block 4. Block 3 uses no attention, and the destination values remain stable at every CoT position of the same step since the operands are fixed and Blocks 1-2 recover the same values each time.

**Proposition 6** (Store results)**.** _Suppose that at every & position_ \(s_\unknown\)_, the full snapshot for the next step--the set of destination addresses_ {_a<sub>d</sub>_} _together with_ bits(_a<sub>d</sub>_) _and the corresponding result words_ bits(_v<sub>d</sub>_)_--is in the residual stream (from Blocks 1-3 evaluated at_ \(s_\unknown\)_). Then T can, at every position_ \(t>s_\unknown\) _within the step, attend to the rightmost &, compute the offset_ \(\delta=^\mathrm{def}t-s_\unknown\)_, and emit the correct_ \(\delta^\mathrm{_th}\) _token of the step’s serialization (a `mem` marker, a # marker, an address bit, a value bit, or the closing &) in constant depth, using one attention layer and one MLP._

_Proof._ **Anchoring at the most recent &.** By construction, & tokens partition the transcript into steps: each step’s serialization is a run of _Cw+D_ tokens following an & (and ends with the next &), where _C_=2_K_ and _D_=3_K_+1 for _K_ the (program-determined) number of memory blocks committed by the active step. An attention head issues a query matching the & token type via Lem. 13, uniquely attending to the rightmost & at position \(s_\unknown<t\) (or to the input boundary token at the very first step). The retrieved value vector is the positional encoding \(\mathrm{PE}(s_\unknown)=\mathrm{bits}(s_\unknown)\). A subsequent MLP computes the within-step offset \(\delta=^\mathrm{def}t-s_\unknown\) from PE(_t_) and \(\mathrm{bits}(s_\unknown)\); this difference ranges over {1_,...,Cw+D_}. The same attention head also retrieves, from the residual stream at \(s_\unknown\), the snapshot (the destination addresses bits(_a<sub>d</sub>_) and result values bits(_v<sub>d</sub>_) for every memory block of the current step, in fixed order) that Blocks 1-3 produced at \(s_\unknown\).

**Selecting and emitting the** \(\delta^\mathrm{th}\) **token.** The serialization layout of a step is fixed once dispatched: a sequence of memory blocks of the form `mem` # \(\langle w\) address bits\(\rangle\) # \(\langle w\) value bits\(\rangle\) at known offsets, followed by a closing &. The MLP converts \(\delta\) to its one-hot encoding \(\mathbf{e}_\delta\in\{0,1\}^{Cw+D}\) and uses it to select among:

(1) the `mem` token when \(\delta\) is the offset of the start of a memory block;<tbc>

(2) a # marker when \(\delta\) is the offset of an address-field or value-field start;<tbc>

(3) an address bit \(b_j=\mathrm{bits}(a_{\mathrm{block}(\delta)})^\top\mathbf{e}_{j(\delta)}\) (Svete and Cotterell, 2024, Lem. B.1) when \(\delta\) falls inside an address field;<tbc>

(4) a value bit \(b_j=\mathrm{bits}(v_{\mathrm{block}(\delta)})^\top\mathbf{e}_{j(\delta)}\) when \(\delta\) falls inside a value field, where \(\mathrm{block}(\delta)\) and \(j(\delta)\in\{1,\dots,w\}\) are the block index and intra-field bit index determined from \(\delta\) alone;<tbc>

(5) the closing & when \(\delta=Cw+D\), which simultaneously triggers the next step’s full Block 1-3 evaluation at that position.

The selected token is emitted as the output at position _t_.

**Why the snapshot is reliable at & positions.** Blocks 1-3 are run at every position _t_ uniformly; what changes across positions is the prefix they see. At an & position \(s_\unknown\), all rightmost-address reads see the previous step’s committed memory blocks (no half-written block of the new step has yet been emitted), so the operand reads are unambiguous and Blocks 1-3 produce the correct snapshot for the next step. At any non-& position within the step’s serialization, the same machinery runs but its rightmost-match reads now collide with the partially emitted memory block of the current step: in particular, a read for any destination address _a<sub>d</sub>_ would retrieve the (possibly partial) freshly written<tbc>

value rather than the operand-time value. Block 4 sidesteps this by anchoring on the rightmost & and copying the snapshot computed there, where only fully committed memory blocks are visible; the local outputs of Blocks 1-3 at non-& positions are disregarded.

**Proposition 7** (Multiplication, division, and modulo via per-iteration memory cells)**.** _Let I be a_ \(\times\), \(\div\)_, or_ mod _instruction with operands a and b. Then T can compute the result of I in_ O(_w_) _Word RAM steps, each costing_ O(_w_) _CoT tokens, for a total of_ O(_w_<sup>2</sup>) _CoT tokens, using only the four-block pipeline above._

_Proof._ **Why** O(_w_<sup>2</sup>) **tokens are necessary.** The standard bit-serial long-multiplication and long- division algorithms run _w_ outer iterations, each updating an _w_-bit intermediate. Compiling the instruction into _w_ flat Word RAM micro-steps that share state through memory yields a \(w\times\mathcal{O}(w)=\mathcal{O}(w^2)\) token budget; each micro-step is exactly the standard four-block pipeline, with no special control flow.

**Per-iteration state in memory.** The program reserves four private memory addresses \(\alpha_P\), \(\alpha_R\), \(\alpha_q\), \(\alpha_\pi\) (constants, fixed at compile time) for the partial product _P_, the running remainder _R_, the partial quotient _q_, and a phase counter \(\pi\), respectively, plus two more \(\alpha_a,\alpha_b\) for the operand snapshot. The compiled implementation of _I_ is a program fragment that

(1) on entry, writes the operands _a,b_ to \(\alpha_a,\alpha_b\), zero-initializes _P,R,q_, and sets \(\pi\leftarrow 1\);<tbc>

(2) executes a loop of _w_ flat micro-steps, each of which reads _a,b_, the current intermediates, and \(\pi\), performs one algorithm iteration, writes the updated intermediates and \(\pi\leftarrow\pi+1\), and branches on \(\pi\);<tbc>

(3) on exit, writes the final result to the destination address.

Each micro-step has compile-time-fixed read and write address sets (entries of \(\{\alpha_a,\alpha_b,\alpha_P,\alpha_R,\alpha_q,\alpha_\pi\}\)), so the operand descriptors and four-block pipeline of Props. 3 to 6 apply unchanged: each micro-step costs O(_w_) CoT tokens.

**Multiplication** (\(a\times b\mathrm{mod}2^w\))**.** Indexing bits LSB-first, micro-step \(\pi\) extracts \(b_\pi=\mathrm{bits}(b)^\top\mathbf{e}_\pi\) in Block 3 and computes \(P'=P+a\cdot b_\pi\cdot 2^\pi(\mathrm{mod}2^w)\). After _w_ micro-steps, \(P=a\times b(\mathrm{mod}2^w)\), and a final step copies _P_ to the destination.

**Division and modulo** (\(a\div b\), _a_mod_b_)**.** Indexing bits LSB-first, micro-step \(\pi\) processes bit \(i=w-\pi\) of _a_ (MSB to LSB). Block 3 extracts \(a_i=\mathrm{bits}(a)^\top\mathbf{e}_i\), computes \(R'=(R\checkmark 1)|a_i\), performs the trial subtraction \(R''=R'-b\), and tests the sign via the high bit of the (_w_+1)-bit result. If \(R''\ge 0\): \(q'=q|(1\checkmark i)\), \(R\leftarrow R''\); otherwise: \(q'=q\), \(R\leftarrow R'\). After _w_ micro-steps, \(q=\lfloor a/b\rfloor\) and _R=a_mod_b_, and a final step copies the appropriate value to the destination.

Both algorithms use O(_w_<sup>2</sup>) CoT tokens via the standard four-block pipeline.

_Remark_ 2 (Why log<sup>2</sup> width is necessary). The Read step above uses \(w=\Theta(\mathrm{log}n)\) heads, each of width \(\Theta(\mathrm{log}n)\), for a total model dimension of \(\Theta(\mathrm{log}^2n)\). Both factors are forced.

_Logarithmically many heads._ To reconstruct bits(_v_) at a single position, one must gather _w_ bits from _w_ distinct earlier positions. Compressing information from a log-growing number of positions into fewer constantly-many heads is infeasible at constant precision: the attention weight at each position is a scalar, so with _o(w_) heads the aggregated output is a fixed-dimensional summary of _o(w_) positions, which cannot faithfully recover all _w_ bits. One could in principle design highly bespoke positional encodings (with L-uniform PEs; cf. London and Kanade (2025) and Svete and Sabharwal (2026)) that pack multiple bits into a single head’s key-query score, but this would substantially complicate the construction and break the clean one-bit-per-head structure; we therefore use \(\Theta(w)\) heads.

Carrying the positional offset bits(_w-t_) in the query already requires \(\theta(1)\) bits of information per head; a constant-width head cannot encode this offset. Hence each head must itself be of growing width.
